query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles synthesized as near-equiatomic high‐entropy alloys preserve structural and chemical stability under high-temperature service regimes because the presence of multiple principal elements creates extensive lattice strain and pronounced local energy barriers that kinetically suppress atomic diffusion and coarsening.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near-equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles (e.g., five-element noble metal or transition metal systems) prepared under low-temperature or low-mobility conditions, ensuring a random, highly dispersed alloy phase.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set of high-entropy (≥5 elements, near-equiatomic) nanoparticles and one set of binary or fewer-element nanoparticles (with otherwise similar synthesis routes). Subject both sets to a controlled thermal treatment (annealing) at temperatures up to 1173 K, representative of catalytic service conditions.
generation.conditions: Service temperatures between 773–1173 K for catalysis (and up to 1923 K for thermoelectric use), under an inert or relevant reactive atmosphere. Synthesis should be carried out by methods that limit precursor atom mobility (e.g., low-temperature reduction or rapid quenching) to freeze in the disordered state.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice strain and local chemical disorder arising from the multiple constituent elements act as structural mediators that hinder atom mobility and sintering.
generation.mechanism: The extensive lattice distortion inherent to the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles raises local energy barriers for atomic diffusion. This sluggish diffusion prevents atom relocation that would enable particle coalescence, phase segregation or growth during high-temperature exposure, thus preserving the desired single-phase and high-dispersion state.
generation.predicted_outcome: After thermal treatment, high-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit minimal particle growth, retain a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution structure, and show less chemical segregation relative to the binary counterparts. Their catalytic activity and thermoelectric properties will be better preserved at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Binary or low-entropy nanoparticles synthesized under similar conditions expected to display more pronounced sintering and phase segregation upon annealing at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective when the synthesis method effectively limits atom mobility (e.g., via rapid quenching or low-temperature reduction) and for near-equiatomic compositions with at least five different elements. If synthetic conditions allow high atomic mobility (such as prolonged high-temperature processing), the stabilizing effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact on diffusion rates and the extent of size stabilization are not yet defined, and potential contributions from support interactions may also affect stability. Thus, exact differences in sintering and phase retention require experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one as a high-entropy alloy (≥5 elements in near-equiatomic ratios) and one as a binary alloy, using a synthesis method that limits precursor mobility. Mount both types on identical supports and subject them to in situ annealing using a transmission electron microscope (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) studies while gradually increasing the temperature to 1173 K. Compare particle size distributions, phase purity and evidence of elemental segregation before and after thermal exposure.
measurements: Phase composition and crystallinity (via in situ XRD)
Elemental mapping to assess segregation (via EDX)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles exhibit similar degrees of sintering, phase segregation or chemical inhomogeneity as observed in the binary alloy samples after annealing at high temperatures, then the hypothesis that lattice strain and local energy barriers in HEAs kinetically suppress diffusion and confer stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.
